So you have the powerful against ordinary families. One was tax cuts for the richest Americans. And the second was putting federalist members of the federalist society into the courts. And the federal society was formed to essentially have the courts find a version of the First Amendment that favored corporate power over ordinary people. So these two things that were the top driving force behind the Trump administration weren't about ordinary families. They were about the powerful. And why does this tension exist? Well, you think about it. When you have a concentration of wealth, that money can be used to hire lobbyists. That money can be invested in elections. That money can be used in media campaigns to change the the essential understanding of an issue on how to frame an issue. It can be used in teams of lawyers that can test things in the courts. And it can be used after you have controllable legislature to change the laws so that the laws continue to favor the more powerful. And there is a point that really represents that completely. It's changing the laws that make it harder for ordinary people to vote. So the voice of the powerful is threatened by the voice of the people. And if it's harder for the people to get to the ballot, it makes it easier for the wealthy and powerful to keep doing the wealthy and powerful thing, which is to make themselves better off. So that is this fundamental tension. There's so much manipulation that can go on. So this is where S1 comes in for the People Act. It says, hey, no, our job under the Constitution here in the Senate, we've taken our oaths of office to defend the constitutional vision of the participation of Americans in the direction of their government. That is government up by and for the people, whether your views are on the right or on the left, you get to participate. And that's the battle we're in the middle of right now.
